newsitem.title: FRANCE: Yeltsin missile gesture steals NATO summit show.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin missile gesture steals NATO summit show.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin surprised NATO leaders on Tuesday by announcing Russia would no longer aim nuclear missiles at their cities, and told U.S. President Bill Clinton he wanted to take further steps to reduce tensions.

Yeltsin's dramatic diplomacy came during a one-day Paris summit at which NATO and Russia signed a pact designed to pave the way for a new security order in Europe, allowing peaceful expansion of the alliance into former communist states of the East with Moscow's acquiescence.
The president initially startled Western leaders by rising to make an unscheduled second speech at the signing ceremony, pledging to remove the warheads from weapons aimed at NATO.

Yeltsin, who has a history of stealing the global spotlight by giving impromptu performances, later clarified his statement through a spokesman and amplified it further at a one-hour meeting with Clinton.
"The president means that the warheads will not be targeted at the states which have signed the (NATO-Russia) Founding Act," Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told reporters.

"In future, the situation is possible when the warheads will be dismantled," Yastrzhembsky said. "I think, judging by everything, this initiative was triggered by the atmosphere of goodwill and welcome which dominates the summit."

Yeltsin told Clinton he was extending an agreement between the Kremlin and Washington not to aim nuclear missiles at each other so that it included the entire territory of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, and offered to discuss other confidence-building measures at expert level, U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger said.
"I think it's a reflection of the momentum of today in which Russia and NATO entered a new era of partnership. It is a step which further reduces tensions," he told reporters.

Asked if U.S. officials had been informed beforehand of Yeltsin's pledge, Berger replied: "No, there was no prior indication that President Yeltsin would make the announcement, but it was a welcome one."
"I think the more significant fact here is that a step was taken in the direction of reducing nuclear tensions, and I think that's important and significant."
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright blamed initial confusion about the extent of Yeltsin's gesture on a "mis- translation."
"We had clarification within a few minutes," she said.

Yeltsin and Clinton agreed at a Moscow summit in early 1993 no longer to target each other's cities, but defence experts said the pact was more symbolic than substantive, noting that retargeting missiles involves only a few computer key strokes and takes a matter of minutes.

"We've always taken the view with respect to our own 'detargeting' agreement with the Russians that it's important, among other reasons, because it assures greater security in moments of crisis not to have warheads targeted," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Yeltsin has caught other leaders off guard with spur-of- the-moment decisions in the past, including taking up the baton to conduct a band during 1994 ceremonies marking the withdrawal of former Soviet troops from Germany and singing off key.

Asked if U.S. officials were concerned about what appeared to be Yeltsin's off-the-cuff policy-making, McCurry said: "President Yeltsin is known to speak his mind at moments like this. I'd say there was nothing out of the ordinary about that."
Yeltsin and Clinton also talked about economic issues during a "very relaxed and very comprehensive" private meeting at the U.S. ambassador's residence in central Paris, Berger said.

As he has previously, the U.S. president promised to support Russian membership in the World Trade Organisation and other top international financial institutions as soon as its parliament made the required legal reforms, the U.S. official said.
